transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I... well, it's a bit difficult to explain exactly, because it's not like a sudden pain or a broken bone, you know? It's more of an absence. I’ve been a social worker for a long time, working with mental health and substance abuse, and I’ve always been very invested in it. I have a master's degree, I’ve always been driven. I used to really care, really connect with my clients and my colleagues. I’d come home and I’d have energy left over for my own life, too. I used to love going to yoga classes, I’d go three times a week, and I’d spend my weekends walking through art galleries, just absorbing the creativity. I even kept a journal, writing down my thoughts and feelings every night. But lately... well, for a while now, actually, it’s like that part of me has just... evaporated. The part that used to reach out to people, that wanted to connect, it's gone very, very quiet. I don't feel that spark of pleasure in my work anymore, or in yoga, or the galleries, or even my journaling. I look at my journal and I just don't have anything I want to say. I'm just... I'm mostly just moving through my obligations, checking boxes, going through the motions because I know I have to, not because I feel any desire to. It's just this heavy, quiet emptiness where my drive and my joy used to be, and that's what finally made me realize I needed to come in and talk to someone.
How long have you been feeling this way, with this emptiness and lack of drive?

Well, if I really trace it back... I'd say it's been about eight months. Yes, eight months, because I can pinpoint it to a very specific event in my personal life. This whole change in how I’m thinking, how I'm working, and just... connecting with people, it all really started since we took my older relative into our apartment. 

It was a huge transition for us. You know, you have your space set up a certain way, your routines, your boundaries between work and home, and then suddenly you're sharing that space with someone older who needs a bit more accommodation and presence. We had to clear out the spare room, which used to be my sort of quiet space where I'd journal or just decompress after a heavy day at the clinic, and we had to reorganize the whole apartment to make it safe and comfortable for them. 

At first, I just thought the lack of energy was from the physical exhaustion of moving furniture and boxes, and the mental load of adjusting to a new living situation. I told myself it was just caregiver fatigue, which I see all the time in my line of work. But the physical work ended, and we got into a rhythm, yet this... this heavy quietness inside me just stayed. It didn't lift. So it's been a solid eight months of waking up and feeling like my drive is just completely tapped out. I kept waiting for it to bounce back, thinking maybe once they were fully settled I'd want to go back to yoga or see my friends, or even just feel invested in my clients again, but... no. It's been eight months of just this flat, empty feeling stretching on and on.
Do you still find pleasure in any activities or things that you used to enjoy before this change?

No, not really... I mean, I really try. I try to think about the things that used to bring me that sense of fulfillment, that little spark, but it's just... not there. Like, I mentioned the yoga, right? I used to love the feeling of stretching out, the quietness of the studio, the way the instructor would talk about breathing into the tight spaces. I used to walk out of there feeling so light. And now, even the thought of unrolling my mat just feels like an impossible task. It’s like... why bother? What’s the point? 

And the art galleries... oh, I used to spend hours just wandering through the local exhibits on a Saturday afternoon. I loved looking at the brushstrokes, trying to figure out what the artist was feeling, the colors... it used to make my mind feel so alive and engaged. But a few weeks ago, I actually forced myself to go to an opening that a colleague recommended. I thought, maybe if I just put myself in that environment, the old feeling would come back. But I stood there looking at this beautiful landscape painting, and I just felt... nothing. Just this blankness. I was just staring at canvas and paint. I ended up leaving after twenty minutes because I felt so disconnected from everyone else there who was chatting and drinking wine and enjoying themselves. 

Even my morning coffee... you know how you have that first cup and it’s just the best thing in the world? The smell of it, the warmth of the mug in your hands... it used to be my favorite part of the day, my little moment of peace before the chaos of the clinic. Now, it’s just hot brown water. I drink it because I need the caffeine to get through my appointments, not because I actually enjoy it. It's like the volume on all the good things in life has been turned all the way down to zero, and I just can't seem to find the dial to turn it back up, no matter how hard I try to force myself to participate in things I know I used to love.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to be alive or wishing you could just disappear during these past eight months?

No, no... I haven't had thoughts like that. I mean, I know what you're asking, being in the field myself. We screen for that all the time, asking clients if they have a plan, if they have intent, if they just wish they wouldn't wake up. But for me, it's not like that. It's not a desire to end things or to disappear, it's more just... a complete lack of desire to *do* things. 

It's strange because, you know, when you work in mental health, you see people who are in so much pain that they just want it to stop, and you see people who feel so overwhelmed by their lives that disappearing feels like the only relief. I've sat across from so many people in that exact headspace, and I've helped them safety plan and find reasons to hold on. So I know what that darkness looks like, I know the shape of it. But what I'm feeling... it's not dark, exactly. It's just gray. 

I don't want to die. I don't sit around wishing I could just vanish into thin air. I still get up, I still feed the cat, I still make sure my relative has their medication sorted out for the week. I'm still functioning, still existing. It's just that the existing part feels so incredibly hollow. Like I'm a car running on fumes, just coasting down a very long, very flat road. I'm not looking to drive off a cliff, I'm just... not enjoying the scenery anymore, and I don't really care where the road goes. But no, to answer your question directly, I haven't had any thoughts of self-harm or suicide. I just want to feel like *me* again, you know? I want to want things again.
Have you noticed any changes in your physical movement or activity level over the past eight months?

Well, physical movement... it's funny you ask that, because it's not so much about the big movements, like I'm not pacing the floors or anything like that, but there are these smaller things. These odd little behaviors that I've noticed, and honestly, they're starting to make me a bit self-conscious, especially given my line of work. 

I've always been a fairly organized person, you have to be to manage a caseload and keep all the documentation straight, but lately... it's different. A few times recently, like during our weekly team meetings at the clinic, or even—and this is the part that really bothers me—even when I'm sitting across from a client, I've caught myself doing these strange, repetitive things. I'll find myself taking the pens from my desk and arranging them in these very exact, specific patterns. Like, I have to line them up perfectly by color or size, and I get so absorbed in making sure the spacing is exactly right. I don't even realize I'm doing it at first, it's just this compulsion to organize them in this very particular way.

And it's not just the pens. I've also found myself... echoing things. Like, a colleague will say something, or a client will express a thought, and before I can even stop myself, I'm repeating the exact phrase they just used. Just muttering it right back. It's not like I'm trying to actively practice active listening or reflect their words back to them therapeutically, it's just... slipping out. And I see the looks on their faces when I do it. People look at me like I've just stepped outside the room somehow, like I'm not fully present or like I've just said something completely bizarre. Which, I suppose, I have. 

It's just so out of character for me. Usually, I'm so dialed in, so focused on the person in front of me, reading their body language, processing what they're saying. But now, it's like my brain is misfiring and making my body do these weird little glitches. I try to catch myself, I really do, but it's like I have to expend so much energy just to sit still and act "normal" during a session, and sometimes these things just leak out anyway. It's incredibly distracting, and honestly, a bit embarrassing. I'm supposed to be the one helping them hold it together, you know? And here I am, lining up highlighters and repeating their sentences like a parrot.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past eight months?

Well, weight... it's interesting you ask about that, because you'd think with everything else going on, with the total lack of interest in things, that my appetite would just completely vanish. I mean, in our field, we always check for those somatic changes, right? Significant weight loss or gain when someone is struggling. But for me... no, my weight has stayed pretty much exactly the same. I step on the scale in my bathroom—it's this old digital one I bought maybe five or six years ago—and the number hasn't really budged. I haven't lost any significant amount of weight at all. 

Which is actually a little surprising to me, honestly, because my relationship with food has definitely changed over these last eight months. Like I mentioned with the coffee earlier, nothing really tastes *good* anymore. I used to love cooking, you know. I'd spend my Sunday afternoons meal-prepping for the week, trying out new recipes, making these vibrant, healthy meals to take to the clinic so I wouldn't end up buying takeout. Now, the thought of chopping vegetables or standing over a hot stove just feels entirely exhausting. It's too many steps. So, I'm eating a lot more convenience foods, things I can just microwave or eat straight out of the package. A lot of toast, maybe some frozen dinners. Sometimes I'll realize it's 7 PM and I haven't eaten since a quick lunch between client sessions, so I'll just pour a bowl of plain cereal and stand in the kitchen eating it. 

But despite all that, despite the fact that I'm just eating purely to sustain myself rather than for any kind of pleasure or culinary enjoyment, my body hasn't really changed. My clothes all still fit exactly the same as they did last year. My work slacks aren't loose, my belts are on the exact same notch they've always been on. So no, no real weight loss to speak of. It's just a very dull, mechanical approach to eating now. I eat because I know my brain needs the fuel to get through the afternoon appointments and I need to keep my blood sugar stable, not because I actually want a meal. But yeah, the scale just hasn't moved.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep over the past eight months?

Sleep... you know, it's funny, because sleep is usually the very first thing to go, isn't it? When I do intakes with my own clients at the clinic, the first thing I ask about is their sleep architecture. Are they having trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, early morning awakenings, nightmares... we look for all of those disruptions because it's such a massive indicator of where their baseline is at. So naturally, I've been hyper-aware of my own sleep habits over these last eight months, just waiting for the other shoe to drop. 

But honestly? No. There haven't been any changes at all. I still go to bed at the exact same time I always have. Usually right around 10:30 PM. I have this whole wind-down routine, which I know probably sounds incredibly rigid, but it's just how I've always operated to manage the stress of the job. I make sure all the screens are off by 9:30, I might sit in the living room for a bit—though lately, I don't really have the interest in reading a book or doing much of anything, so I just sort of sit there on the couch—and then I brush my teeth and I'm out like a light by 11:00. 

And I sleep right through the night. I don't wake up tossing and turning, I don't wake up in a panic. My alarm goes off at 6:15 AM every single morning, and I get up. It's almost frustrating, in a way? Because I feel so drained and hollowed out during the day, like I mentioned, that you'd think my sleep would be completely fragmented, or on the flip side, that I'd be sleeping fourteen hours a day just to escape the grayness of it all. But my body just stubbornly sticks to its usual seven-ish hours like clockwork. 

I do have very good sleep hygiene, I suppose. I have these heavy blackout curtains in my bedroom, and I use a white noise machine—the classic kind, you know, the one with the actual physical fan inside it, not the digital sound loops, because those digital ones always have that tiny little micro-skip at the end of the track that my brain fixates on and it drives me absolutely up the wall. So anyway, I turn the fan on, I close the curtains, and I sleep perfectly fine. So no, to make a long story short, my sleep hasn't changed a bit. It's really just the waking hours that feel so different.
Have you felt like you're moving more slowly than usual?

Moving slowly... you mean like physically? No, I don't think so. I haven't noticed any kind of slowing down like that. 

You know, in our field, we look for that all the time, don't we? The psychomotor retardation. When a client comes in and they just look like they're moving through molasses, taking ten seconds just to answer a simple question or physically dragging themselves into the chair. It's such a heavy, visible symptom. But for me, no, I haven't experienced anything like that at all. 

I still walk down the hall to the waiting room at the exact same brisk pace I always have. Our clinic has this incredibly long, poorly designed hallway—it’s an old converted municipal building, so the layout makes absolutely no sense, just these long stretches of beige linoleum—and I have to walk all the way from my office in the back corner to the front reception area to get my clients. I do that back-and-forth trip maybe six or seven times a day. And I'm not dragging my feet or taking any longer to get there than I did a year ago. I'm not getting winded or feeling like my limbs are made of lead. 

Even with smaller movements, it's the same. I still type up my progress notes just as fast, my fingers fly across the keyboard at the exact same words-per-minute they always have. When I'm cooking—well, microwaving things now, I guess—I'm not moving in slow motion. So the actual mechanical speed of my body, the physical momentum... that’s all completely intact. It’s not a speed issue. Like I said before, it’s really just those weird, unprompted little movements, the organizing the highlighters and the echoing, rather than feeling weighed down or sluggish. The machinery is running at the normal speed, it's just... doing the wrong things sometimes. But no, I wouldn't say I'm moving slowly.
Do you often feel guilty or blame yourself for things that have happened?

Guilt... well, that’s another one of those classic markers we screen for, isn't it? Feelings of worthlessness or excessive, inappropriate guilt. It's practically drilled into us in grad school when we're learning to do biopsychosocial assessments. You look for that heavy, ruminative self-blame where a client is taking responsibility for things completely outside their control, or just relentlessly beating themselves up over minor infractions. 

But for me? No. I don't really experience that at all. Honestly, it's almost the opposite, which is a little disturbing in its own way when I take a step back and analyze it. Because logically, objectively speaking, there are things right now that I probably *should* feel a little guilty about. Like my work, for instance. I'm a social worker, I have clients who rely on me to be present and empathetic and sharp. And lately, with this total lack of interest and this... this grayness I've been describing, I know I'm not giving them my best self. 

Just last week, I had a session with a substance abuse client I've been seeing for over two years, and I caught myself completely zoning out while she was talking about a pretty significant family conflict. The old me, the me from a year ago, would have agonized over that. I would have brought it straight to my clinical supervision group, I would have felt terrible, I would have spent the whole weekend blaming myself for being a bad clinician and doing her a massive disservice. 

But now? I just sort of... noticed I was checked out, redirected my attention, and that was it. There was no emotional fallout. No guilt. No self-flagellation. I went home and ate my microwave dinner and didn't give it a second thought. And it's the exact same in my personal life. I'm not keeping up with my friends, I haven't called my sister back in three weeks, and I just... I don't feel bad about it. 

It’s like the emotional bandwidth required to feel guilt just isn't there anymore. Guilt requires you to care deeply about the impact of your actions, and right now, I just feel so disconnected from everything that I can't even muster up the energy to blame myself for dropping the ball. It’s just a very flat, neutral feeling. I don't sit up at night ruminating over past mistakes or thinking I'm a terrible person. So, no, I'm not carrying around any guilt or self-blame. I'm just sort of... existing alongside the things that happen, if that makes sense.
Are there any activities that you still enjoy or find pleasure in, no matter how small they may seem?

Enjoyment... pleasure. No. Honestly, no. And, you know, that’s actually the crux of it. That specific absence is what finally brought me in to see you. Because it’s one thing to feel a little burned out—we all get compassion fatigue in social work, it’s practically a given when you're carrying other people's heavy emotional baggage all day long. You learn to expect a certain ebb and flow in your energy levels. But this is entirely different. I feel like... I feel like the part of me that used to reach for people, the part that used to genuinely take pleasure in my life, has just gone very, very quiet. 

I used to have such a full, engaged routine. I loved my work, of course, I found deep satisfaction in connecting with my clients and helping them navigate their crises. But I also had my own outlets to keep myself grounded. I used to go to this yoga studio a few blocks from my apartment, usually three times a week, just to stretch out the tension and center myself. I loved going to art galleries on Sunday afternoons, too. I'd spend hours just wandering through the exhibits, taking my time to really look at the compositions and read every single artist statement on the wall. I even kept a journal. I’ve been journaling religiously since grad school, using these specific fine-tip pens I'd order online, just to process my thoughts and decompress before bed. 

But now? I haven't even unrolled my yoga mat in months. It's just gathering dust in the corner of my bedroom. The thought of going to a gallery just feels like... I don't know, like staring at a blank wall. It just doesn't register as something desirable anymore. Even the journaling, which used to be my ultimate safe space, my daily ritual, just feels completely empty. I've tried opening the notebook a few times, but I just sit there staring at the paper and I have absolutely nothing to say. 

That whole vibrant, engaged part of my personality has just flatlined. So, no, there aren't any activities I'm enjoying, not even the small ones. I’m mostly just moving through obligations now. I get up when my alarm goes off, I go to the clinic, I do the paperwork, I come home, I microwave my dinner. It’s just this endless, repetitive series of mechanical tasks. I'm just fulfilling these obligations so the basic structure of my life doesn't collapse, but there is absolutely no joy or spark in any of it anymore.
Do you still enjoy spending time with friends and family?

Friends and family... yeah, I mean, it’s exactly like what I was just saying about the yoga and the galleries and my work. It all falls under that same... that same overarching absence. 

Like I mentioned a minute ago, what finally brought me in to see you—the real tipping point for me making this appointment—is that I feel like the part of me that used to reach for people has just gone very, very quiet. I brought up my sister earlier, how I haven't called her back in weeks. We used to talk on the phone every single Sunday evening. It was our ritual. She lives a few states over, so it was our way of staying connected, and I genuinely used to look forward to it. I'd make a cup of herbal tea, sit on the couch, and we'd just chat for an hour about everything and nothing. But now? When her name pops up on my phone screen, I just stare at it. I let it go to voicemail. 

And it's the same with my friends. I have a close-knit group of friends from my MSW cohort, and we usually try to get together for dinner at least once a month to decompress and talk shop. They’ve been trying to organize a get-together for three weeks now, and I just keep making up excuses. It's not that I'm angry with them, or that we had a falling out, or anything dramatic like that. It's just that the desire to connect, the actual pleasure I used to get from being around them and hearing about their lives, is completely gone. 

Socializing just feels like another heavy task on a to-do list. Like I said, I’m mostly just moving through obligations now. If I do happen to go to a dinner or pick up the phone, it’s strictly mechanical—I do it only because I feel like I *have* to, just to maintain the absolute bare minimum so people don't start worrying or asking too many questions. But there’s no joy in it. I just sit there, nodding at the appropriate times, using all my active listening skills to fake engagement, and just waiting for it to be over so I can go back to my apartment and be by myself. It’s exhausting, honestly, trying to pretend that I'm still a person who wants to engage, when really, that whole social drive has just completely shut down.
Have you been feeling restless or fidgety lately?

Restless... no. No, not at all. Actually, it’s quite the opposite, really. When you ask about being restless or fidgety, my mind immediately goes to the clinic. I picture the clients I see in the waiting room—the ones who are pacing back and forth, endlessly bouncing their knees, picking at their cuticles or wringing their hands. You know, that classic psychomotor agitation you see with severe anxiety or as a side effect of certain medications. I observe that kind of physical restlessness all day long in my line of work, so I'm very attuned to what it looks like and what it feels like to be in the room with it. 

But for me? Personally? No, I'm not experiencing anything remotely like that. If anything, I'm just incredibly still. Probably too still, to be honest. Like I was saying before about just going through the motions and coming home to eat my microwave dinner... once I sit down on my couch in the evening, I just stay there. I don't feel the need to move or get up or shift around. There's no internal motor running, no nervous energy looking for an outlet. 

I remember a time, maybe a year or two ago, when I used to have a little bit of that normal nervous energy. Like, if I had a big case presentation or a difficult court appearance for a client, I might tap my pen on the desk or shift my weight around in my chair while I was prepping my notes. But now, with this heavy, flat feeling I've been describing, there's just no energy available to be restless. It takes a certain amount of internal drive, or at least a certain level of anxiety or tension, to be fidgety, doesn't it? And I just don't have that bandwidth right now. 

I'm just... stationary. I sit at my desk at the clinic, I sit on the train on my commute, I sit in my apartment, and I barely move unless I absolutely have to for a specific task. My body just feels very heavy and anchored in place. So, no, there’s no pacing, no leg bouncing, no fidgeting whatsoever. Just a whole lot of sitting perfectly still.
Do you feel sad most of the day?

Sad? No. No, I wouldn't use the word sad at all. It's actually an important distinction, I think. Because as a social worker, you know, I spend a significant portion of my week assessing clients for depression. I'm constantly looking for that pervasive sadness, the tearfulness, the heavy grief that just sort of hangs over a person like a dark cloud. I sit across from people every single day who are profoundly sad, who are just completely drowning in despair, so I have a very clear, professional and personal understanding of what sadness looks like and how it operates in the room. 

But for me? What I'm going through? It's not sadness. Sadness is an active emotion. It's a feeling. It means there's still something there, some kind of emotional resonance happening inside you, even if it's painful. What I'm experiencing is just... a void. It's an absence. It's not that I'm walking around all day wanting to cry, or feeling down, or dwelling on these heavy, negative thoughts. There really aren't any negative thoughts. Honestly, there aren't many thoughts at all in that emotional realm. It's just a complete and utter flatness. 

In a weird way, if I were sad, I almost think I'd welcome it. I really do. Because at least it would mean I was feeling *something*, you know? It would mean the machinery is still working, even if it's hurting. But this is just a total erasure of feeling. Like my emotional baseline has been completely wiped clean, and someone just pulled the plug on the whole system. So if you're asking if I'm crying or feeling blue or grieving something... no, absolutely not. I'm just existing in this very neutral, gray, quiet space where an emotion like sadness doesn't even have the energy to register.
Are there any activities that you find pleasurable or enjoyable?

Pleasurable activities... well, I think this really gets back to the heart of what I’ve been trying to explain since I sat down. Like I mentioned earlier, what finally brought me in to see you—the absolute main reason I picked up the phone and made this appointment—is that I feel like the part of me that used to reach for people, and the part of me that used to take pleasure in things, has just gone very, very quiet. 

It’s completely faded out across the board. Take my work, for instance. Being a social worker in the mental health and substance abuse field is incredibly demanding, you know that, but I used to find it so deeply rewarding. I used to thrive on the complex cases, the feeling of helping a client navigate a crisis. I'd leave the clinic tired, but fulfilled. Now? There's no pleasure in it whatsoever. I’m mostly just moving through obligations. I do the intakes, I write the notes, I file the reports, but the spark is completely gone. 

And it’s the exact same story with my personal life and my hobbies. I used to do Vinyasa yoga three times a week. I had this beautiful, warm studio I went to downtown, with exposed brick walls and these big windows, and I genuinely loved the feeling of stretching and the mindfulness of it. It was my sanctuary. But now, my yoga mat is just gathering dust rolled up in the corner of my bedroom. I look at it and feel absolutely nothing, no pull to use it at all. 

I also used to spend my Saturday afternoons wandering around art galleries. I'd grab an iced coffee and just lose myself in the new exhibits for hours, analyzing the compositions, letting myself feel inspired by other people's creativity. Now, the mere thought of going to a gallery just feels like... a chore. Just another heavy task. 

Even something as simple and private as journaling, which I've done religiously since grad school. It used to be my primary way of processing the heavy trauma I hear from clients all day, a safe place to decompress and organize my mind. I have stacks and stacks of filled notebooks on my bookshelf. But I haven't written a single word in months. The desire to even pick up a pen, to reflect on anything, is just completely absent. So, no, to answer your question... there really aren't any activities I find enjoyable anymore. Everything that used to bring me joy has just become another item on a checklist that I'm forcing myself to get through.
Are there any small pleasures in life that you still look forward to?

Small pleasures... you mean like, a good cup of coffee in the morning, or a nice sunset? I know I just sort of bombarded you with my whole list of lost hobbies—the yoga, the galleries, the journaling—but really, it’s the exact same answer for the small things, too. 

Like I was saying a minute ago, this is exactly what finally brought me in here. It’s that this... this profound quietness has just completely taken over everything. The part of me that used to reach for people, whether it was a deep conversation with a friend or just a pleasant chat with the barista at the corner cafe... it's gone very, very quiet. I don't look forward to any of it. Even at work, where I used to at least enjoy the small moments, like a client having a tiny breakthrough or just the quiet satisfaction of organizing my desk for the day... now I’m mostly just moving through obligations. 

I wake up, I look at the clock, and I just see a series of tasks. Getting dressed is a task. Making tea is a task. Commuting is a task. There’s no... there’s no anticipation, no little reward at the end of the day. I know it sounds incredibly bleak, and I know I'm probably repeating myself, but it really is just so pervasive. Whether it's a big weekend outing to a museum or just the small pleasure of reading a chapter of a book before sleep... the pleasure part is just entirely switched off. I'm just going through the motions to get to the end of the day, every single day.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure from activities that you used to enjoy?

Well, yes. I mean, I feel like I've been saying exactly that for the last ten minutes, haven't I? I know I can get a bit long-winded, it's an occupational hazard of being a social worker, we're trained to talk and process and unpack every little detail... but yes, that is precisely the issue. That is the exact reason I'm sitting in this chair right now. 

It's just... like I said, what finally brought me in, what made me realize I couldn't just keep ignoring this and hoping it would pass like some sort of phase, is that I feel like the part of me that used to reach for people, the part that used to genuinely take pleasure in my work, in my yoga practice, in wandering through those art galleries, even in just sitting quietly and journaling... it has all gone very, very quiet. It's like the volume knob on my capacity for joy was just slowly turned all the way down to zero. 

And it's incredibly frustrating, because intellectually, I know I used to love those things. I know I used to look forward to them. I have the memories of enjoying them. But the actual feeling? The internal reward? It's completely absent. I'm mostly just moving through obligations now. I wake up, I go to work, I come home, I stare at the wall. Everything is just a task to be completed. There's no spark, no engagement, no... no life in it anymore. It's just a constant, exhausting routine of going through the motions without any of the payoff that makes life actually worth living. So, yes, to put it simply, I am completely unable to experience pleasure from the things I used to enjoy.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure from most activities most of the time?

Yes... yes, most of the time. Honestly, all of the time. I know I’m sounding like a broken record here, and I apologize for that, but I just really need you to understand the depth of this. Because as a mental health professional myself, I know the diagnostic criteria, I know the checkboxes you're mentally ticking off right now, but living it... living it is entirely different from reading about it in the DSM. 

It’s just... it’s exactly what I’ve been trying to articulate since I walked through your door. What finally brought me in, what made me realize I couldn't just keep pushing through and pretending everything was fine, is that I feel like the part of me that used to reach for people, the part that used to genuinely take pleasure in my work with my clients, in my yoga practice, in those Saturday afternoons at the galleries, even in just sitting down and journaling at the end of the day... it has all gone very, very quiet. It's a silence that just echoes through my entire life now. 

There's no exception to it. It's not like I have a bad day at work but then I come home and find solace in a good book or a hot bath. It's constant. From the moment I open my eyes in the morning until I finally manage to fall asleep at night, I’m mostly just moving through obligations. Everything is a 'must-do', a 'should-do', a 'have-to-do'. There's absolutely no 'want-to-do'. The capacity for enjoyment, for that little spark of satisfaction or joy that makes the heavy lifting of life bearable... it’s just completely absent, in almost every single activity, almost every single minute of the day. So, yes, to answer your question definitively... yes, I am unable to experience pleasure from most activities, most of the time. Really, all the time.

But there’s no joy in it. I just sit there, nodding at the appropriate times, using all my active listening skills to fake engagement, and just waiting for it to be over so I can go back to my apartment and be by myself. It’s exhausting, honestly, trying to pretend that I'm still a person who wants to engage, when really, that whole social drive has just completely shut down.

patient.answer:
Sad? No. No, I wouldn't use the word sad at all. It's actually an important distinction, I think. Because as a social worker, you know, I spend a significant portion of my week assessing clients for depression. I'm constantly looking for that pervasive sadness, the tearfulness, the heavy grief that just sort of hangs over a person like a dark cloud. I sit across from people every single day who are profoundly sad, who are just completely drowning in despair, so I have a very clear, professional and personal understanding of what sadness looks like and how it operates in the room. 

But for me? What I'm going through? It's not sadness. Sadness is an active emotion. It's a feeling. It means there's still something there, some kind of emotional resonance happening inside you, even if it's painful. What I'm experiencing is just... a void. It's an absence. It's not that I'm walking around all day wanting to cry, or feeling down, or dwelling on these heavy, negative thoughts. There really aren't any negative thoughts. Honestly, there aren't many thoughts at all in that emotional realm. It's just a complete and utter flatness. 

In a weird way, if I were sad, I almost think I'd welcome it. I really do. Because at least it would mean I was feeling *something*, you know? It would mean the machinery is still working, even if it's hurting. But this is just a total erasure of feeling. Like my emotional baseline has been completely wiped clean, and someone just pulled the plug on the whole system. So if you're asking if I'm crying or feeling blue or grieving something... no, absolutely not. I'm just existing in this very neutral, gray, quiet space where an emotion like sadness doesn't even have the energy to register.
